thesis: Match verification to claim and separate generation, evaluation, acceptance and records.

ideas.statement: Truth, calculation, completeness, safety, compliance and usefulness need distinct checks.
External evidence and calibrated abstention differ from repeated self-approval.

evidenceAndExamples.statement: “I asked another model, and it said it was correct.” The sentence can describe a useful check. It can also describe two systems that learned the same regularities, read the same mistaken premises, and prefer the same convincing answer.

We need not reject automated evaluation. We must ask how its verdict relates to what we want to verify. A style evaluator, a program test, and a proof checker do not have the same authority over the same question.

“This paragraph is clearer” requires an editorial criterion and an audience. “This number is the column’s sum” requires data and calculation. “This source supports the claim” requires access to the passage and interpretation. “The program satisfies the property” requires a specification and a verification method. “This decision is fair” also requires normative judgments, not only facts.

A single score from one to ten can hide all these differences. We propose a verification worksheet listing separately factual truth, computational correctness, compliance with the requirement, completeness, safety, and usefulness for the purpose. Not every task requires every component. That choice itself must be explicit.

An answer can be factually correct and useless. It can be useful and incomplete. It can satisfy the literal request and produce unwanted consequences. Saying “it is good” without specifying the dimension returns us to the prize with changing value.

Zheng and colleagues studied LLM evaluation in MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, also identifying sensitivities such as answer order and preferences for certain presentation forms. Automated judges can be useful for comparison and screening, but their verdict must be calibrated and systematic errors tracked. They do not become independent sources of truth merely because their role is called “critic.” [33]

A fictional example: two answers explain the same result. One is short and correct. The other is long, fluent, and introduces a false premise. An evaluator too strongly oriented toward the impression of completeness may prefer the second. The solution is not always to prefer short texts, but to check decisive premises separately from style.

We can randomize the order of alternatives, hide authorship, use concrete rubrics, and periodically compare the verdict with human evaluations or external tests. These measures reduce some errors, not all. Several diverse models can offer useful perspectives, but diversity must be demonstrated in error patterns, not assumed from product names.

Huang and colleagues reported limits to self-correcting reasoning without external feedback on the models and tasks tested. The paper’s title should not be turned into an eternal law about all systems. By contrast, CRITIC research by Gou and colleagues explores self-correction assisted by tools and feedback. The important distinction is between reformulating the same evaluation and introducing new evidence, such as executing a calculation or consulting a source. [34] [35]

If we ask ten times for a product and choose the majority answer, we use a different mechanism from performing the multiplication. If we request the bibliography for a claim ten times, the number of answers does not prove the papers exist. Mechanization must target the relevant relationship, not the multiplication of approvals.

A model can say “I am 95% sure.” For that number to be useful, we should know what it means across a family of comparable tasks. When the system expresses high confidence, how often is it actually right? What happens on different data? What severe errors are hidden by a good average?

In a protocol proposed here, we collect tasks with verifiable answers and compare confidence with results. We separate task types and error severity. We retain an option to abstain: sometimes the correct evaluation outcome is “there is not enough evidence.” A percentage generated in the current conversation does not substitute for this calibration.

Nor does a good average rate automatically approve a high-stakes decision. A system can be excellent on a thousand details and get wrong the one detail that changes a recommendation. Acceptance criteria must be connected to consequences and the possibility of repair.

The book’s general proposal has four roles: the generator produces candidates; evaluators seek evidence and errors; an acceptance rule decides what may be used; a log preserves what was actually checked. The roles can be automated to different degrees. What matters is that the generator cannot rewrite the criterion on its own after seeing the result.

Independence does not mean absolute isolation. The evaluator can explain the failure, and the generator can repair it. But the history remains, protected tests remain, and the distinction between “proposed” and “accepted” does not disappear.

We are not building a new oracle. We are building a process in which an answer must be able to show why it deserves belief. For some questions, the evidence will be strong. For others, it will remain limited. A system that recognizes this difference is more useful than one that sounds equally certain in every situation.

objectionsAndQualifications.statement: Judge diversity is empirical, no eternal self-correction law follows, consequences matter beyond averages.

audit.notes: Complete chapter read; preserve proposed concepts, empirical limits and non-diagnostic distinctions.
